title: Finite equivariant covers of schemes with open geometric orbits
statement: Let $k$ be a field, let $P$ be a smooth group scheme of finite type over $k$, and let $Q$ be a group scheme of finite type over $k$ [def-weil-field, def-pc-scheme, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Group schemes have multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group-object identities. Let $u:P\to Q$ be a finite surjective group homomorphism [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism]. Let $W$ be a finite-type $k$-scheme with a $Q$-action. Suppose that for every algebraically closed extension $\Omega/k$, $W_\Omega$ is a finite disjoint union of open geometric $Q_\Omega$-orbits: on each nonempty piece any two points over any algebraically closed extension $\Omega'/\Omega$ are related by an element of $Q(\Omega')$. Let $V$ be a geometrically reduced finite-type $k$-scheme, meaning that $V_{k'}$ is reduced for every field extension $k'/k$, with a $P$-action and a finite surjective morphism $v:V\to W$ satisfying $v(pz)=u(p)v(z)$ as an equality of morphisms on $P\times_k V$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. Then $V$ is smooth over $k$. Moreover, for every algebraically closed extension $\Omega/k$, the connected components of $V_\Omega$ are a finite disjoint union of open geometric orbits of $(P_\Omega)^0$, the connected component containing the identity of $P_\Omega$ [lem-sfb-lft-field-group-neutral-component, def-weil-connected-scheme]; equivalently each connected component is one such orbit, with transitivity on points over every algebraically closed extension of $\Omega$. Empty $V=W$ is allowed. No affineness, commutativity, reducedness of $Q$ or $W$, or perfectness of $k$ is assumed.

source.place: Proposition 4.2.3 (OCR 4,2,5), printed p.59, geometric-orbit argument after normalization, isolated in its field form. Orbit machinery: Milne, Algebraic Groups (2017), Lemma 1.64 and Propositions 1.65–1.66, printed pp.26–28, literature/milne-algebraic-groups_iAG2017.pdf. This lemma includes the finite-equivariant orbit comparison that the paragraph uses; it is not the potential-normalization theorem. Local Anantharaman archive WANTED; primary scan https://www.numdam.org/article/MSMF_1973__33__5_0.pdf

proof.text: Fix an algebraically closed extension $F/k$ and base change all data to $F$. Finite type, finite morphisms, surjectivity and smoothness survive this base change by the cited permanence lemmas. Geometric reducedness gives reducedness of $V_F$ directly from its definition. All finite-type $F$-schemes here are Noetherian, since a field is Noetherian. Their open subschemes are Noetherian and of finite type: their inclusions are quasi-compact open immersions and finite type composes. Thus the given open pieces $W_j$ and $V_j=v_F^{-1}(W_j)$ are finite type. We henceforth work over $F$ and omit the subscript. Empty pieces may be discarded; if there are no pieces there is nothing to prove.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text: The finite surjection $u$ is onto on $F$-points. Indeed its fibre at a rational point is a nonempty finite scheme over $F$, so it has a closed point; the residue-field lemma makes that point rational. The prescribed transitivity of $Q(F)$ on each $W_j(F)$ therefore implies transitivity of $P(F)$. Apply the general orbit lemma to the $P$-action $(p,y)\mapsto u(p)y$ on $W$: the reduced orbit $O_w$ of any $w\in W_j(F)$ has support all of $W_j$. First, $b_w^{-1}(W_j)$ is open in $P$ and contains every closed point $p$ of $P$, since $p$ is rational and $pw=u(p)w\in W_j(F)$ as the orbit piece $W_j$ is $Q$-stable; its closed complement has no closed point, hence is empty, so $|O_w|\subseteq W_j$. Next, the closure of $|O_w|$ contains all rational points of $W_j$, hence all of $W_j$ by their density; $|O_w|$ is open in this closure, so $W_j\setminus|O_w|$ is closed in $W_j$ and has no rational point, hence is empty. In particular $W_j$ is equidimensional of some finite dimension $d_j$, and, writing $H=P_w$, the dimension formula gives $d_j=\dim P-\dim H$. Nilpotents in $W_j$ do not change its topological dimension.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text: Put $P^0=(P_F)^0$. The neutral-component theorem gives a clopen geometrically irreducible finite-type subgroup, compatible with every further field extension. It is smooth since it is open in the smooth group $P$. We will use the following elementary dimension observation. If $L$ is any finite-type $F$-group and $K\subset L$ a nonempty open subgroup, its cosets by $L(F)$ cover $|L|$: the closed complement of their union, if nonempty, would have a rational closed point. Quasi-compactness gives a finite coset cover. Translation identifies every coset with $K$, so $\dim L=\dim K$ by finite-union dimension. In particular $\dim P^0=\dim P$, and for every closed finite-type subgroup $J\subset P$, $J\cap P^0$ is an open subgroup and $\dim(J\cap P^0)=\dim J$. Rational-point detection here uses density of closed points and their residue fields. Finite-union dimension follows directly because an irreducible closed set contained in a finite union of closed sets lies in one; an open subgroup is also closed, since its other cosets form its open complement.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text: For $z\in V_j(F)$ put $w=v(z)$, $H=P_w$ and $J=P_z$. Equivariance gives $J\subset H$, and $H$ acts on the finite fibre $V_w$. Its underlying points are finite and rational. For each point of the $H(F)$-orbit of $z$ choose $h_i\in H(F)$ carrying $z$ to it. The fibres of $H\to V_w$, $h\mapsto hz$, over those points are the closed cosets $h_iJ$, by the group identities. These cosets cover all rational points of $H$, hence all of $|H|$, by closedness of their finite union and density of rational closed points. Translation makes their dimensions equal, so finite-union dimension yields $\dim H=\dim J$. This uses no flatness or reducedness of $V_w$, $H$, or $J$.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text:
Apply the general orbit lemma to the $P^0$-action on $V$. Its stabilizer at $z$ is $J\cap P^0$ by the fibre-product definition. Steps 2–4 give
$$\dim(P^0z)=\dim P^0-\dim(J\cap P^0)=\dim P-\dim J=\dim P-\dim H=d_j.$$
Thus every rational-point $P^0$-orbit in $V_j$ has dimension $d_j$, is smooth and locally closed, and is irreducible because $P^0$ is connected. The action preserves $V_j$: each prescribed piece of $W$ is a geometric $Q$-orbit, and equivariance carries its inverse image to itself. Scheme-theoretic restriction to these open pieces follows by the unique factorization through an open subscheme.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text: The morphism $V_j\to W_j$ is finite by base change. Its scheme-theoretic fibres have dimension zero when nonempty: on an affine chart a finite algebra over a field is finite-dimensional, and its quotient by a prime is a finite-dimensional domain, hence a field (multiplication by any nonzero element is injective and therefore surjective). Thus no strict chain of primes exists. Apply the fibre dimension bound with $n=0$ to obtain $\dim V_j\leq d_j$. This bound does not require flatness or reducedness of $W_j$.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text: Let $O=P^0z\subset V_j$. If its boundary in $V_j$ were nonempty, that locally closed finite-type subset would contain a rational closed point $y$; invariance puts $O_y$ in the boundary. The boundary inequality in the orbit lemma gives $\dim O_y<\dim O=d_j$, whereas step 5 gives $\dim O_y=d_j$. Therefore $O$ is closed in $V_j$. It is irreducible of dimension $d_j$, so it is an irreducible component: if properly contained in a larger irreducible closed subset, a maximal chain of length $d_j$ in $O$ followed by that larger subset would contradict step 6. There are only finitely many irreducible components. All rational-point $P^0$-orbits are therefore closed components, and they are pairwise disjoint by the orbit lemma. There are finitely many, and their union is closed and contains every rational point of $V_j$, hence is all of $V_j$ by density of closed points. The complement of any one is a finite union of closed orbits, so each is open. Their irreducibility makes each connected; a connected subset cannot meet two disjoint clopen pieces. Consequently these are precisely the connected components of $V_j$. The finitely many $V_j$ form a disjoint open partition and hence are clopen in $V$, so these are also precisely the connected components of $V$.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text: The source $V_F$ is reduced. On each clopen orbit support, its open-subscheme structure is therefore reduced and agrees with the canonical reduced orbit structure, by uniqueness of reduced induced closed subschemes. The orbit lemma makes these open subschemes smooth. They cover $V_F$, so $V_F\to\operatorname{Spec}F$ is smooth by the local definition of smoothness. The map $\operatorname{Spec}F\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is affine, quasi-compact, flat and surjective: faithful flatness is the field-extension lemma, and affine flatness is the flat-affine criterion. Smooth fpqc base descent now gives smoothness of $V/k$.

source.place: Propositions 1.65(b),(c), 7.4(b), 7.5 and 7.6, printed pp.27,139–140; Appendix A.11, A.14–A.15, A.71–A.73, pp.569,582. Orbit dimension from the faithfully flat orbit map and its stabilizer fibres; Stacks varieties.tex Tag 0B2L, lemma-dimension-fibres-locally-algebraic.

proof.text: For any algebraically closed extension $E/F$, the orbit lemma gives transitivity of $P^0(E)$ on the $E$-points of each of the clopen components just constructed. The neutral-component base-change equality identifies this group with $((P_E)^0)(E)$. Since $F/k$ was an arbitrary algebraically closed extension, this proves exactly the asserted geometric transitivity for every $V_F$ and every further algebraically closed extension. Empty $V=W$ gives an empty finite orbit decomposition and a smooth empty morphism.
